title: Mixed Methods Studies That Mix
intro: Most teams that say they run mixed methods are just running separate studies and putting them in one deck. Real mixed methods means the methods inform each other — planned from the start, integrated during analysis.

learn.title: Parallel tracks ≠ mixed methods
learn.text:
Running a survey and a few interviews and combining them in one report is **parallel research**, not mixed methods.

**Mixed methods** means:
→ Methods answer the **same question** from different angles
→ Methods **inform each other** — one shapes the next
→ Integration is **planned before** data collection
→ Findings **change because of how the methods interacted**

The test: if one method alone would have reached the same result, it wasn't mixed.

Synthesis left until after data collection is too late. You end up stacking findings instead of letting one method challenge the other.

left.label: Parallel Research
items: Separate studies, combined in a report
Each method answers its own question

try.q: You ran a survey and 5 interviews separately, then put both in one deck. Is this mixed methods?
options: No — it's parallel research unless the methods informed each other
Yes — you used both qualitative and quantitative methods
Yes — any combination of methods is mixed methods
Only if you had more than 30 survey responses
try.explain: Mixed methods requires the methods to interact — one shaping the other. Running them separately and combining at the end is parallel research.

learn.title: The four designs
learn.text:
**1. Exploratory Sequential (qual → quant)**
Interviews or field work first, then a survey to size what you found.
Example: Patient interviews reveal different mental models of blood pressure graphs. A survey measures how common each model is.

**2. Explanatory Sequential (quant → qual)**
Start with a quantitative pattern, then use qual to explain it.
Example: A new onboarding raised activation but lowered retention. Interviews revealed users felt rushed.

**3. Concurrent Triangulation (qual + quant in parallel)**
Both at once, integrated during analysis by looking for alignment or conflict.
Example: A usability test collects task success rates, eye-tracking, and post-task surveys — analyzed together.

**4. Embedded Design (one primary + one supporting)**
One method drives, another is layered in.
Example: A MaxDiff survey ranks features; open-text responses after each task explain the choices.

try.q: A dashboard metric shows a 20% drop-off. You run follow-up interviews to understand why. Which design is this?
options: Explanatory Sequential — quant pattern first, then qual to explain it
Exploratory Sequential — qual first, then quant
Concurrent Triangulation — both at the same time
Embedded Design — one supporting the other
try.explain: Starting with a quantitative finding and then using qualitative research to explain the 'why' is Explanatory Sequential.

learn.title: When it fits and how to do it right
learn.text:
**Good fit when:**
→ You need both behavior AND intent
→ You expect conflicting signals from different sources
→ An expensive decision needs both scale and nuance
→ Edge cases or regulated contexts need extra rigor

**Poor fit when:**
→ The question is narrow and one method already answers it
→ Timeline can't support real integration
→ Stakeholders can't engage with layered findings

**Six-step process:**
1. Start with the decision, not the methods
2. Map each question to a method
3. Align sample sizes upfront
4. Plan integration points before collecting data
5. Prevent cherry-picking — show conflicts explicitly
6. Build time to reconcile contradictions

**Key principle:** Don't average conflicting findings. Surface the tension. A feature users rate highly in surveys but struggle with in testing → they like the concept but not the execution.

left.label: Don't
items: Use mixed methods when one method suffices

right.label: Do
items: Show where findings conflict and why
Match method to the decision you need

try.q: A feature scores high in a survey but frustrates users in interviews. What should you do?
options: Surface the tension: users like the concept but struggle with the execution
Average the results — it's probably fine
Trust the survey because it has a larger sample
Trust the interviews because they're more detailed
try.explain: Conflicting findings are a signal, not a failure. Users may like the idea but struggle with the implementation — that points to a redesign, not removal.

test.q: What's the key difference between parallel research and mixed methods?
options: In mixed methods, the methods inform each other and are integrated from the start
Mixed methods always uses more participants
Parallel research is qualitative, mixed methods is quantitative
Mixed methods takes longer to run
test.explain: Mixed methods means integration is planned upfront and methods shape each other. Parallel research runs methods separately and combines at the end.

test.q: You want to understand why users are dropping off a specific page. Analytics show the pattern but not the cause. Which mixed methods design fits?
options: Explanatory Sequential — start with quant, then qual to explain
Exploratory Sequential — start with qual, then quant to size it
Concurrent Triangulation — both at the same time
Embedded Design — one method inside another
test.explain: You already have a quantitative pattern (drop-off) and need qualitative work to explain why. That's Explanatory Sequential.

test.q: When should you NOT use mixed methods?
options: When the question is narrow enough that one method already answers it
When the decision is expensive
When you expect conflicting signals
When you need both behavior and intent
test.explain: If one method answers the question cleanly, adding another just adds complexity without insight. Mixed methods is for questions that genuinely need multiple angles.

test.q: What should you do with contradictory findings from different methods?
options: Surface the contradiction and investigate what it means for the decision
Trust whichever method had the larger sample size
Average the results for a balanced view
Discard the weaker finding
test.explain: Contradictions are valuable signals. A feature users love in concept but struggle with in practice points to an execution problem, not a data problem.

test.q: The self-check for real mixed methods includes 5 criteria. Which of these is one of them?
options: Findings changed because of how the methods interacted
At least 100 participants were used across methods
Both methods used the same data collection tool
Results were presented in a single slide deck
test.explain: If one method alone would have reached the same result, the study wasn't truly mixed. The methods should produce different — and richer — findings together.
